newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - ITT sees early return on Desert Inn.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - ITT sees early return on Desert Inn.

text.p: ITT Corp this year will start to see a return on its $160 million renovation of the Desert Inn resort in Las Vegas, Chief Operating Officer Robert Bowman said.
Bowman, who is also ITT's president, made his comments in an interview with Reuters on Thursday after the company reported its 1996 fourth-quarter and full-year earnings.
The Desert Inn resort opened December 26. Bowman said ITT was billing it as "the first five-star luxury resort in Las Vegas," complete with a golf course and spa.
Some analysts have said the casino might be located too far away from Las Vegas' busiest area. However, Bowman said there's a reason for its relative seculsion.
"It's not a walk-in casino," Bowman said. "It's not a place that's going to have 5,000 people a day walk in there. It's geared toward people going there as a destination."

Bowman did not specify how much the resort would add to the company's revenue in 1997 -- a year that might hold some acquisitions for ITT. The acquisitions would likely be in hotels, rather than in gaming, Bowman said.

"The problem with buying casinos is there's no shareholder enhancement," Bowman said. "You buy at a high multiple and that's what it is forever. With the (casinos) we build, we can add the features we want."

ITT earned $0.57 per share in the quarter, compared with $0.59 in the year-ago period, beating the mean estimate of $0.56 per share from 11 analysts surveyed by First Call. The company also said it earned $2.11 per share for the year, compared with $1.76 in 1995, in line with First Call's $2.11 estimate.

ITT reported overall fourth-quarter gaming revenues of $305 million in the fourth quarter, compared with $318 million in 1995. While a shortfall, it did not take analysts by surprise. What did was the company's hotel results, which surged.
The company said its overall hotel revenue jumped to $1.24 billion from $1.11 billion, a rise of 11.2 percent.
"That was way above expectations," said Jason Ader, an analyst at Bear Stearns.
Bowman said the jump in hotel revenue was fueled more by hotel rate increases than a rise in occupancy rates -- a trend he said was likely to continue in 1997.
"In 1996 we did it with rate; we'll see about 1997," he said. "Margins are better on rate."
Bowman would not speculate on earnings estimates for the company in its typically slow first quarter or for the full year.
He would not comment on speculation the company would sell its $550 million stake in Alcatel when it is allowed to do so after June 30.
"We have certainly put a higher priority in investing in gaming than holding that stock," he said. "Certainly, our priorities are in gaming."
